html:
This post is a continuation of the previous post on convergence and compactness. Here we study the important notions of weak and weak* convergence in details, and to provide ourselves a fundamental framework for studying compactness methods in PDEs. Major reference is Terry's notes, and also several discussions found in Mathstackexchange.

1.1. Compactness in the norm topology

We recall first the Heine-Borel theorem for metric spaces.

Theorem 1 (Heine-Borel) Let (X,d) {(X,d)}(X,d) be a metric space. Let K⊂X {K\subset X}K⊂X. The following are equivalent:

*- K {K}K is sequential compact;

  • K {K}K is compact, i.e. every open cover has a finite subcover;
  • K {K}K is complete, and totally bounded, i.e. for each ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0 there is a finite number of metric balls of radius ϵ {\epsilon}ϵ covers K {K}K.*

Several simplifications can be made if the metric space X {X}X is a finite dimensional normed vector space over R {\mathbb{R}}R. First,

Proposition 2 X {X}X as a finite dimensional normed vector space will be automatically complete.

In fact, more is true: any two norms on a finite dimensional vector space are equivalent, and we can identify this space with Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn equipped with the ℓ1 {\ell^{1}}ℓ1-norm. Given this, we can show

Proposition 3 K⊂X {K\subset X}K⊂X is bounded if and only if totally bounded.

It suffices to show for the closed cube Q=[−1,1]n {Q=[-1,1]^{n}}Q=[−1,1]n is totally bounded. If not, let {Uα}α∈A {\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in A}}{Uα​}α∈A​ be a collection of infinite open balls of the same radius that cover Q {Q}Q but without a finite subcover. Because n {n}n is finite, we can subdivide Q {Q}Q into 2n {2^{n}}2n closed cubes of equal sides. By pigeon hole principle, at least one of the cubes requires infinite cover. Call this cube Q1 {Q_{1}}Q1​. Continuing, we have a nested sequence

Q1⊃Q2⊃⋯\displaystyle Q_{1}\supset Q_{2}\supset\cdotsQ1​⊃Q2​⊃⋯

which by completeness satisfies ⋂n=1∞Qn={x} {\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}Q_{n}=\{x\}}⋂n=1∞​Qn​={x} for some x∈Q {x\in Q}x∈Q. But then the sequence will eventually lies in one covering ball. This is enough to deduce a contradiction. Finally, since complete subsets are also closed, we conclude the usual Heine-Borel theorem that K⊂X {K\subset X}K⊂X if and only if K {K}K is closed and bounded.
In the case of infinite dimensional Banach space (since compact sets are neccesarily complete, a Banach space in fact gives us more compact sets), the norm topology is so strong that it forces the compact sets to be "almost finite dimensional''.

Proposition 4 Let V {V}V be a Banach space and K⊂V {K\subset V}K⊂V. Then K {K}K is compact if and only if K {K}K is closed and bounded, and for each ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, K {K}K lies in the ϵ {\epsilon}ϵ-neighborhood of some finite dimensional subspace W⊂V {W\subset V}W⊂V.

This follows by a direct application of Theorem 1.

Example 1 By Proposition 4, we see that in ℓp(N) {\ell^{p}(\mathbb{N})}ℓp(N), 1≤p<∞ {1\leq p<\infty}1≤p<∞, a subset K {K}K is compact if and only if K {K}K is closed and bounded, and also uniformaly integrable at the spatial infinity, in the sense that for each ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, there is n>0 {n>0}n>0 such that

(∑m>n∣f(m)∣p)1/p≤ϵ\displaystyle \left(\sum_{m>n}|f(m)|^{p}\right)^{1/p}\leq\epsilon(m>n∑​∣f(m)∣p)1/p≤ϵ

for all f∈K {f\in K}f∈K. Hence we see that the "moving bump'' (en)n=1∞ {(e_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}}(en​)n=1∞​ is not compact, despite being closed and bounded in ℓp(N). {\ell^{p}(\mathbb{N}).}ℓp(N).

We conclude this section with a construction of F. Riesz, which leads to the remarkable converse to the statement that closed unit ball is compact if the space is finite dimensional. Thus in particular, compact sets in an infinite dimensional space must have empty interior.
Consider an infinite dimensional normed vector space X {X}X, and W⊂X {W\subset X}W⊂X a finite dimensional subspace. Take x∈X {x\in X}x∈X. Then there is y∈W {y\in W}y∈W such that it is a distance minimizer:

This entails the following property of the unit sphere S {S}S in X {X}X: pick any x0∈S {x_{0}\in S}x0​∈S, and let xn {x_{n}}xn​ be a point such that ∥x−w∥≥1 {\|x-w\|\geq1}∥x−w∥≥1 for all w∈span{x0,…xn−1} {w\in\text{span}\{x_{0},\dots x_{n-1}\}}w∈span{x0​,…xn−1​}. 1.2. The weak and weak* topologies

Recall that a topological vector space V {V}V is a vector space with a topology such that vector space operations are continuous with respect to that topology. We shall refer to this given topology as the strong topology on V {V}V. This topology gives rise to the notion of dual space V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ of V {V}V, defined to be the space of all continuous linear functionals on V {V}V.
If the space is finite dimensional, its dual space can be identified with the space itself by a choice of basis {e1,…,en} {\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}}{e1​,…,en​} and the map

Φ:ei↦Φ(ei)=δi,\displaystyle \Phi:e_{i}\mapsto\Phi(e_{i})=\delta_{i},Φ:ei​↦Φ(ei​)=δi​,

where δi {\delta_{i}}δi​ is the Kronecker delta. The choice of basis had identified V {V}V with Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn, on which the product topology can be shown to be equivalent to any norm topology. Yet it is also the weakest topology that makes any λ∈V∗ {\lambda\in V^{*}}λ∈V∗ continuous, since a linear combination of δi {\delta_{i}}δi​'s is essentially the same with the corresponding linear combination of coordinate projection πi {\pi_{i}}πi​'s. The situation is quite different for infinite dimensional spaces. We make the following definition.

Definition 5 The weak topology on a topological vector space V {V}V is generated by all the semi-norms (i.e. a norm except that ∥v∥=0 {\|v\|=0}∥v∥=0 does not neccessarily imply v=0 {v=0}v=0) of the following form

∥⋅∥λ:∥v∥λ=∣λ(v)∣,\displaystyle \|\cdot\|_{\lambda}:\|v\|_{\lambda}=|\lambda(v)|,∥⋅∥λ​:∥v∥λ​=∣λ(v)∣,

for λ∈V∗ {\lambda\in V^{*}}λ∈V∗. The basic open sets generated by ∥⋅∥λ {\|\cdot\|_{\lambda}}∥⋅∥λ​ are of the form

{v∈V:∣λ(v)∣<c},\displaystyle \{v\in V:|\lambda(v)|<c\},{v∈V:∣λ(v)∣<c},

for c>0 {c>0}c>0. A sequence (vn)n=1∞ {(v_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}}(vn​)n=1∞​ converging to v∈V {v\in V}v∈V in the weak topology satisfies

λ(vn)→λ(v)\displaystyle \lambda(v_{n})\rightarrow\lambda(v)λ(vn​)→λ(v)

for all λ∈V∗ {\lambda\in V^{*}}λ∈V∗. We call the sequence (vn)n=1∞ {(v_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}}(vn​)n=1∞​ converges weakly to v {v}v, and denote it by

vn⇀v.\displaystyle v_{n}\rightharpoonup v.vn​⇀v.

By this definition, all λ∈V∗ {\lambda\in V^{*}}λ∈V∗ is continuous in the weak topology, since λ {\lambda}λ is continuous in the topology generated by its own semi-norm ∥⋅∥λ {\|\cdot\|_{\lambda}}∥⋅∥λ​. Also, the weak topology is easily seen to be the weakest of this kind (i.e. contains fewest open sets). Thus it is weaker than the strong topology.
In a similar spirit,

Definition 6 The weak* topology on the dual space V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ of a topological vector space V {V}V is generated by all the semi-norms

∥⋅∥v:∥λ∥v=∣λ(v)∣,\displaystyle \|\cdot\|_{v}:\|\lambda\|_{v}=|\lambda(v)|,∥⋅∥v​:∥λ∥v​=∣λ(v)∣,

for v∈V. {v\in V.}v∈V. Similarly, a sequence (λn)n=1∞ {(\lambda_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}}(λn​)n=1∞​ converging to λ∈V∗ {\lambda\in V^{*}}λ∈V∗ in the weak* topology satisfies

λn(v)→λ(v)\displaystyle \lambda_{n}(v)\rightarrow\lambda(v)λn​(v)→λ(v)

for all v∈V {v\in V}v∈V. We call the sequence (λn)n=1∞ {(\lambda_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}}(λn​)n=1∞​ converges weak-starly to λ {\lambda}λ, and denote it by

λn⇀∗λ.\displaystyle \lambda_{n}\rightharpoonup^{*}\lambda.λn​⇀∗λ.

Note that weak* topology on V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ depends on which predual V {V}V we use, so one cannot talk about the weak* topology unless the predual is specified or there is no confusion in the context.
By making use of the bidual (V∗)∗ {\left(V^{*}\right)^{*}}(V∗)∗, we can also talk about the weak topology on V∗ {V^{*}}V∗, and so on. The relation between the definitions of these topologies can be schematically shown as follows:

Because of the embedding V↪(V∗)∗ {V\hookrightarrow\left(V^{*}\right)^{*}}V↪(V∗)∗(which uses Hahn-Banach theorem), the weak* topology on V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ is weaker than the weak topology on V∗ {V^{*}}V∗.
From now on we shall be mainly interested in case V {V}V is a normed vector space.

Remark 1 In probability literature people usually refer to the weak-star convergence of measures as weak convergence of measures or vague convergence of measures, perhaps because the dual spaces of measure spaces are seldom considered.

The first question regards to the notion of weak and weak-star convergence is that if their limits, if exist, is unique. This is non-trivial since the topology generated by each individual semi-norm is non-Hausdorff (since each one has a non-trivial kernel). That altogether they generate a Hausdorff topology is due to the Hahn-Banach theorem.

Proposition 7 Let V {V}V be a normed vector space. Then the weak and weak* topologies on V {V}V and V∗ {V^{*}}V∗are Hausdorff.

Proof: By Hahn Banach, if λ(v)=0 {\lambda(v)=0}λ(v)=0 for all λ∈V∗ {\lambda\in V^{*}}λ∈V∗, then v=0 {v=0}v=0. □ \Box□

Lemma 10 Let V {V}V be a Banach space. Then the closed unit ball in V {V}V is closed in the weak topology; also, the closed unit ball in V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ is closed in the weak* topology.

Note that the statement for unit sphere is certainly false (more or less a paraphrase of that strict inequality can hold in Corollary 9).

Theorem 11 (Banach-Alaoglu) Let V {V}V be a normed vector space. Then the closed unit ball of V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ is compact in the weak* topology.

Some additional care is needed for its sequential counterpart.

Theorem 12 (Sequential Banach-Alaoglu) Let V {V}V be a separable normed vector space. Then the closed unit ball of V∗ {V^{*}}V∗ is sequentially compact in the weak* topology.
